lesson.title: Separa los Colores: A Crayon Color-Sort
lesson.subject: spanish

contentBlocks.text: Sol dumped out a whole box of crayons! Let's sort them into color piles — and then count how many crayons landed in each one.
Say each color out loud as you make its pile: put every red crayon with rojo, every blue one with azul, every yellow one with amarillo. Keep going with verde, blanco, and negro.
Now count each pile out loud — uno, dos, tres... How many crayons are rojo? How many are azul? Use the numbers you already know, all the way up to diez.
You sorted every crayon by color and counted each pile — rojo, azul, amarillo, verde, blanco, negro! Tomorrow we play 'Veo veo,' the Spanish way to play I-spy.

objectives: Sort objects into six color groups, naming each color in Spanish as the group is made
Count each color group aloud in Spanish, reusing numbers uno through diez from the last two weeks
materialsNeeded: A box of crayons, or any mixed pile of small objects in several colors (blocks, beads, pom-poms)
Six spots, cups, or sheets of paper to sort onto
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Pour out a box of crayons (or mixed small objects) and set up six sorting spots with Sol.
2. Pick up a crayon, name its color in Spanish, and start its pile — rojo here, azul there — coaching your child to echo each color and add to the right pile.
3. Work through all six colors: rojo, azul, amarillo, verde, blanco, negro.
4. Once everything is sorted, count each pile out loud together in Spanish — uno, dos, tres — bringing back last week's numbers up to diez.
5. Ask '¿Cuántos crayones rojos?' and let your child answer with the number.
6. Complete the on-screen speed-drill activity together, cheering each correct match.
7. Close by asking: 'Which color pile had the most crayons?'
differentiationTips: Struggling: sort into just three color piles — rojo, azul, amarillo — and count only up to cinco
Ready for more: after sorting, line the piles up from smallest to largest and name each color and its count
The crayons do not need to be perfectly sorted — naming the color and counting the pile is the goal, not tidy piles
teacherGuide.answerKey: This is a spoken sorting-and-counting activity — success looks like your child naming each color in Spanish while sorting and counting each pile aloud with last week's numbers. In the speed-drill game, each English color word matches its Spanish counterpart: red → rojo, blue → azul, yellow → amarillo, green → verde, white → blanco, black → negro.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Extends week 5's WA-WL-2015.1.2 target by having the child produce each color word spontaneously while sorting, and deliberately recycles weeks 3-4's numbers uno-diez in the counting step — the scope-and-sequence's own design for this Day 4 — so earlier vocabulary stays live instead of being taught once and dropped.
